sources.title: Pacific Islander Biography (Australian National University): Tupaia, by Ben Finney
sources.supports: Tupaia, a high-born priest and navigator from Ra'iātea, joined Cook's Endeavour in 1769, described Tahitian navigation, and died in Batavia (Jakarta). The entry says Cook drew the chart from Tupaia's list of islands and bearings.

sources.title: Natural History Museum, London: On tour with Tupaia (interview with Anne Salmond)
sources.supports: Tupaia was born about 1725 on Ra'iātea, was a priest of 'Oro and a keeper of navigation knowledge, and died in Batavia on 11 November 1770. Navigators learned star paths and also read winds, currents, clouds and birds.

sources.title: University of Potsdam: Tupaia's Map (research project by Lars Eckstein and Anja Schwarz)
sources.locator: Project description and reading of the chart
sources.supports: The chart was made in stages in 1769 and 1770. European readers found far islands placed side by side and southern islands in the north. Eckstein and Schwarz (2019) read 'avatea' (noon) at the centre as north, and read the islands as voyaging routes. Later critics are named.

sources.title: Knowable Magazine: Reading a Pacific navigator's mysterious map (2021)
sources.supports: The original chart is lost and copies survive. The 2019 reading is debated: Anne Di Piazza and Erik Pearthree read it as many sets of sailing directions, and Anne Salmond says the certainty is overstated. Navigators from Tahiti and Ra'ivavae say work with Indigenous experts is essential.

cards.title: Tupaia of Ra'iātea
cards.text: Tupaia was born about 1725 on Ra'iātea, in the Society Islands. He was a priest and a keeper of navigation knowledge. After warriors from Bora Bora took his island, he lived on Tahiti. In 1769 he joined James Cook's ship Endeavour, guided it through the islands, and explained to the crew how his people found their way at sea. He died in Batavia (now Jakarta) in 1770.
cards.limits: Almost everything written about Tupaia in his lifetime was written by Europeans on the ship. His own words reach us only through their notes.

cards.title: The chart and its first readers
cards.text: In 1769 and 1770, a chart of more than seventy Pacific islands was made with Tupaia. The original is lost; copies survive. European readers found islands thousands of kilometres apart drawn side by side, and southern islands drawn in the north. One of the ship's scientists suggested Tupaia had invented islands. In the twentieth century, the chart was used to argue that Polynesians could not have sailed on purpose.
cards.limits: The sources do not agree on who drew the lines: some say Tupaia, some say Cook drew from Tupaia's list of islands and directions. Some island names were written down by people who did not speak Tahitian well.

cards.title: A new reading, and a debate
cards.text: In 2019 Lars Eckstein and Anja Schwarz proposed a new way to read the chart. At its centre is the Tahitian word for noon. At noon in the southern Pacific the sun is to the north, so they read the centre as 'north', seen from a canoe, not from above. They read the islands as routes: from each island, face the noon sun and read the direction to the next island on the route. Other researchers disagree. Some read the chart as many separate sets of sailing directions. Anne Salmond says the new reading is more certain than the evidence allows. Navigators from Tahiti and Ra'ivavae say the chart cannot be read well without Pacific experts.
cards.limits: This is a scholarly proposal, not a settled fact. No reading can ask Tupaia what he meant.

missions.title: The Chart Read Upside Down
missions.knowledgeQuestion: When a map follows rules we do not know, how can we tell a misreading from a mistake?
missions.stake: For two hundred years this chart was used to say that Pacific navigators could not sail on purpose. A label in the Lantern House will be read by every visitor.

journal.title: The Chart Read Upside Down
journal.text: I read about Tupaia of Ra'iātea and the chart made with him in 1769. Its first readers called it wrong, because it did not follow their rules. A new reading says its centre means noon, and north, seen from a canoe. Others disagree. I wrote a label that says what we know and what we do not.
